1) For the company, the IPO was great. They raised more money than they original thought with the both the amount of shares offered and IPO price increased.

2) The stock closed up 17% which is above the 10-15% threshold to call an IPO of this size successful.

3) The not so great news is the stock opened at +34% peaked a few minutes thereafter at +39% and then closed at +17%. A successful IPO sees the stock close higher than the open. This shows that investors who did not get an allocation are more eager to buy than those looking to sell the initial IPO pop and in this case, now that they finally have liquidity.

4) This decline in Anthropic’s stock over the day is likely the cause of the S&P going from up 1.3% in the morning to flat at the 11:49AM open of the IPO to down 2.0% by the close.

text:
I’ve presented the $MRVL - for- $LITE merger proposal as a prime example of what can go wrong when a company uses its own stock to buy another company’s stock.  In just over a month, $MRVL’s stock has dropped by -45%, which has cut the +24% premium being paid for $LITE to a -41% discount vs $LITE’s stock price before the announcement. This occurs because of massive dilution to the acquiring company’s stock, plus arbitragers pre-selling shares of the acquirer rather than wait for the deal to close in 12-18 months.  

The same dynamic is likely when $SPCX offers a +24% premium for $TSLA using SPCX stock as currency:  TSLA investors will get a short-term pop on the deal headline and then experience quick downward pressure on $TSLA stock as investors sell $SPCX to try to lock in profits.

I would bet most $LITE investors would love to roll back the clock to Oct 28 when their stock was trading at $914 before MRVL’s offer to pay a +24% premium which on paper amounted to $1,132/share ($914 + 24%).  Instead $LITE stock is now DOWN -41% since the deal announcement to just $535/share today (-41% from $914 instead of a +24% premium).  If history repeats, TSLA at $374 today plus a +24% premium paid in SPCX shares (on paper worth $464/share) could be worth -25% less within a month ($280/share) given what could amount to 50% dilution to $SPCX, which could trade down by less than $MRVL since it’s not a pure AI play.

zh_summary: Cullen Roche 解釋基本銀行會計：存款對持有人是資產、對銀行是負債；準備金是銀行資產、聯準會僅對銀行的負債，並非對存款人。個人無法持有準備金，只有銀行可以。提領現金是持有聯準會負債的唯一方式。
en_summary: Cullen Roche explains basic bank accounting: deposits are assets for holders and liabilities for banks; reserves are bank assets and Fed liabilities to banks only, not to depositors. Individuals cannot hold reserves; only banks can. Cash withdrawal is the sole way to hold a Fed liability.
text:
This is basic accounting. When you have a bank deposit you hold an asset and the bank has a liability. Reserves are an asset for the bank and a liability of the Fed. But the Fed's liability is to the bank, not to you. You don't have a claim on reserves because they aren't your asset and they aren't the bank's liability to you. Your claim is on the bank, full stop.

You can't even hold reserves. Only banks and a handful of other institutions with Fed accounts can. When you send money to someone at another bank, your bank settles with their bank in reserves. Your deposit goes away and they get a new one, but the reserves never touch your hands.

The one time you end up holding a Fed liability is when you withdraw cash. Your bank swaps reserves for paper currency and hands it to you. That's a Fed liability, but it's a different one. It isn't reserves.

SPY is −5.55% over the last 20 trading days. QQQ is −9.06%. Study of 54 largest US-listed IPOs since 2007 shows mega-IPOs haven't drained liquidity; market did better than usual. text:
Anthropic starts trading tomorrow. $81.3 billion at $83 a share. The largest IPO in history, ahead of SpaceX's $75B in June.

The market has already paid for it. SPY is −5.55% over the last 20 trading days. QQQ is −9.06%.

The question now: does the drain keep going once $81 billion is in one stock, or was the selling the drain?

We tested it. 54 of the largest US-listed IPOs since 2007. SPY and QQQ forward returns from each listing-day close.

In the 20 trading days after listing, mega-IPOs haven't drained liquidity. The market has done better than usual.

-SPY 20-day forward: +1.90%, 83% win rate (p < 0.0001)
-QQQ 20-day forward: +2.44%, 80% win rate (p = 0.0001)

SPY on any random day: +0.78% over 20 days. After a mega-IPO it beats its own baseline by +1.12% (p = 0.004).

The $15B+ tier: Visa +5.16%, GM +3.62%, Meta +3.59%, Alibaba -6.09%. Three of four positive.

Now the live tests. 2026 gave us two IPOs bigger than anything in the study:

1. SpaceX ($75B, June 12): SPY +1.36%, QQQ -0.23% over 20 days.
2. SK hynix ($26.5B, July 10): SPY +2.43%, QQQ -0.34%.

SPY rose both times, short of the +1.90% average. QQQ was flat both times. No drain. But no tech-led rally either.

Our study starts at the listing, so it can't tell us whether the selling was caused by the IPO. The closest precedent is Meta in 2012: SPY fell −4.98% in the 20 days before, then rose +3.59% in the 20 after. 

The caveat: Anthropic is 3.7x Alibaba, the largest IPO in our historical sample. Two live tests

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on why the company offered buyouts to around 60,000 employees:

The buyouts were meant to give employees a sense of agency in making their own career choices.

Microsoft isn't treating software engineers as obsolete. Software engineering will "thrive," but the way teams are organized and the work engineers do will change significantly with AI.

Employees will increasingly become managers of AI agents and systems that produce the work, with this shift expected across all jobs.

One Microsoft team of just 11 developers building Cowork now builds "a software factory that builds the product," rather than building the product directly.

As a 51-year-old incumbent, Microsoft isn't an AI-first company. The transition to AI-driven workflows will take longer than many expect, and some employees may choose to leave.

AI is here to stay but here’s my view:

AI is going to make humans more - not less - valuable.    

Your boss will spot the “AI ideas” a mile away.

Original and individual thoughts and ideas will win the day.   Wandering around.  Spontaneous moments.  

Travel agents will keep making a comeback (they have been for a few years).

Elon Musk predicts 100% of superintelligence compute will be in space, and says Tesla and SpaceX would “probably” be better together:

“If you look into the future, orbital compute is really going to be where things scale to.”

“In the future, the amount of superintelligence compute that is on Earth will round down to 0% and superintelligence compute in space will round up to 100%.”

“Now remember these words, because that sounds like a preposterous thing to say.”

“I think superintelligence compute [on Earth] will be less than 0.4% of compute. Therefore, orbital compute will round up to 100%. And I think this is a relatively easy prediction to make, and it’s simply a matter of time before that happens.”

Would Tesla and SpaceX be better together?

“Probably yes. Now, this is not like let’s merge the companies no matter what. These require shareholder votes, which may or may not succeed, at least in the case of Tesla.”

“I can’t just drag them into a non-economic merger that is bad for them, because I’ll obviously get sued.”

“It really is just a question of, do SpaceX and Tesla execute better together and create more value than if they’re apart?”

• EUR 3m cross-currency basis is -2.1bp—no offshore funding panic yet. But the onshore plumbing is tightening.
• Gold -3%, silver -7%, copper -11% this month. Hard assets are being sold for cash—the classic liquidity signature.
• Indonesia rupiah at record low 18,204/USD, but EM FX broadly stable. Stress is concentrated, not systemic.
